case_name: Ramdas Bhikaji Chaudhari v Sadanand and Others
facts: This appeal by special leave is directed against a judgment of the Bombay High Court acquitting the respondents of the charge under s. 16(1)(a)(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act.
The respondents were convicted under s. 16(1)(a)(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act and sentenced to 6 months' R.I. and fined Rs. 2000/- as modified by the Sessions Judge in appeal.
The High Court accepted all the facts proved in the case and found that the confectionary drops sold by the accused to the Food Inspector by way of sample contained coal tar dye.
A few admitted facts may be mentioned here.

In the first place the decision of this Court in Rajal Das Guru Namal Pamanani v. State of Maharashtra 1974 Indlaw SC 55, (supra) was reconsidered by a larger bench of 5 Judges who over-ruled the aforesaid decision in the case of State of Kerala etc. v. Allassary Mohammed etc. etc. (supra) and held that Rule 22 was purely directory and must always be construed to have been so.
It was further held that it was for the Public Analyst to say whether the quantity of the sample sent to him was sufficient or not for making necessary analysis.
issues: Whether the acquittal by the High Court was legally erroneous
petitioner_arguments: As at the time when the respondents were acquitted the previous decision of the Court in Rajal Das Guru Namal Pamanani's case 1974 Indlaw SC 55 held the field, it is not a fit case where we should exercise our discretionary power under Art. 136 to set aside the order of acquittal particularly when the case was launched against the respondents as far back as 1971.

Even though the previous decision of this Court was over-ruled by this Court in the case of State of Kerala v. Alassary Mohammed (supra), yet the previous decision was the law laid down by this Court under Art. 141 of the Constitution and, therefore, the judgment of the High Court was correct.

The later decision of this Court in State of Kerala v. Alassary Mohammed (supra) has clearly decided the point of law against the view taken by the High Court and as a logical consequence thereof the acquittal of the respondents was wrong on a point of law.
respondent_arguments: As at the time when the respondents were acquitted the previous decision of the Court in Rajal Das Guru Namal Pamanani's case 1974 Indlaw SC 55 held the field, it is not a fit case where we should exercise our discretionary power under Art. 136 to set aside the order of acquittal particularly when the case was launched against the respondents as far back as 1971.

Even though the previous decision of this Court was over-ruled by this Court in the case of State of Kerala v. Alassary Mohammed (supra), yet the previous decision was the law laid down by this Court under Art. 141 of the Constitution and, therefore, the judgment of the High Court was correct.
court_reasoning: The later decision of this Court in State of Kerala v. Alassary Mohammed (supra) has clearly decided the point of law against the view taken by the High Court and as a logical consequence thereof the acquittal of the respondents was wrong on a point of law.
This Court refused to interfere on special ground peculiar to the cases before them.

In similar situations in the case of the State of Bihar v. Hiralal Kejriwal and Anr 1959 Indlaw SC 106., this Court refused to exercise its discretionary jurisdiction under Art. 136 of the Constitution and did not order the continuance of the criminal proceeding any further.
holding: The judgment of the High Court is vitiated by clear error of law and cannot be sustained.
We hold that the respondents should be convicted under Sec. 16(1)(a)(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act and sentence them to fine of Rs. 2,000/- each, in default 6 months' R.I..
